1
李孝伯李沖
Li Xiaobo; Li Chong
2
李孝伯，趙郡人也，高平公順從父弟。 父曾，少治鄭氏禮、左氏春秋，以教授為業。 郡三辟功曹不就，門人勸之，曾曰：「功曹之職，雖曰鄉選高第，猶是郡吏耳。 北面事人，亦何容易。 」州辟主簿，到官月餘，乃歎曰：「梁叔敬有云：州郡之職，徒勞人耳。 道之不行，身之憂也。 」遂還家講授。 太祖時，徵拜博士，出為趙郡太守，令行禁止，劫盜奔竄。 太宗嘉之。 并州丁零，數為山東之害，知曾能得百姓死力，憚不入境。 賊於常山界得一死鹿，謂趙郡地也，賊長責之，還令送鹿故處。 隣郡為之謠曰：「詐作趙郡鹿，猶勝常山粟。 」其見憚如此。 卒，贈平南將軍、荊州刺史、栢仁子，諡曰懿。
Li Xiaobo came from Zhao Commandery and was a paternal cousin of Duke Shun of Gaoping. His father Zeng had studied Zheng's Rites and the Zuo Tradition of the Spring and Autumn Annals in his youth and earned his living as a teacher. The commandery summoned him three times to serve as Assistant Officer, but he refused. When his disciples urged him to accept, Zeng said, "The post of Assistant Officer may be called the top choice of the district, but it is still only a commandery clerk. To face north and serve another person — how could that be easy? The province then summoned him as Registrar, but after little more than a month in office he sighed and said, "Liang Shujing once remarked that provincial and commandery posts do nothing but exhaust a man. When the Way does not prevail, that is one's own concern." He then returned home to lecture and teach. During the reign of Emperor Daizu, he was summoned and appointed Erudite, then sent out as Administrator of Zhao Commandery. His orders were enforced without exception, and bandits and robbers fled the region. Emperor Taizong praised him for it. The Dingling tribes of Bing Province had long been a menace to Shandong, but knowing that Zeng could command the people's utmost loyalty, they feared to enter his territory. When bandits found a dead deer in the Changshan borderlands and mistook the spot for Zhao Commandery, their chief rebuked them and ordered the deer returned to where it had been found. A neighboring commandery composed a ballad about it: "A fake Zhao Commandery deer is still better than Changshan grain." Such was the fear he inspired. When he died, he was posthumously appointed General Who Pacifies the South and Inspector of Jing Province, ennobled as Baron of Bairen, and given the posthumous name Yi.
3
孝伯少傳父業，博綜羣言。 美風儀，動有法度。 從兄順言之於世祖，徵為中散，世祖見而異之，謂順曰：「真卿家千里駒也。 」遷祕書奏事中散，轉侍郎、光祿大夫，賜爵南昌子，加建威將軍，委以軍國機密，甚見親寵。 謀謨切祕，時人莫能知也。 遷比部尚書。 以頻從征伐規略之功，進爵壽光侯，加建義將軍。
In his youth Xiaobo inherited his father's learning and mastered a wide range of texts. He had a handsome bearing, and his every movement conformed to propriety. His older cousin Shun recommended him to Emperor Shizu, and he was summoned to serve as Palatial Attendant. When the emperor met him, he was struck by his quality and said to Shun, "Truly a thousand-li colt of your house." He was promoted to Palatial Attendant for Memorials in the Secretariat, then transferred to Gentleman and Grand Master for Splendid Happiness. He was ennobled as Baron of Nanchang, given the additional title General Who Establishes Might, entrusted with military and state secrets, and greatly favored. His counsels and plans were kept utterly secret, and people of the time could not know them. He was transferred to Minister of the Ministry of Revenue. For his repeated service on campaign and his achievements in strategy, he was advanced to Marquis of Shouguang and given the additional title General Who Establishes Righteousness.
4
真君末，車駕南伐，將出彭城。 劉義隆子安北將軍、徐州刺史、武陵王駿，遣將馬文恭率步騎萬餘至蕭城。 前軍擊破之，文恭走免，執其隊主蒯應。 義隆聞大駕南巡，又遣其弟太尉、江夏王義恭率眾赴彭城。 世祖至彭城，登亞父冢以望城內，遣送蒯應至小市門，宣世祖詔，勞問義恭等，[1]并遣自陳蕭城之敗。 義恭等問應：「魏帝自來以不？ 」應曰：「自來。 」又問：「今在何處？ 」應曰：「在城西南。 」又問：「士馬多少？ 」應曰：「中軍四十餘萬。 」駿遣人獻酒二器、甘蔗百梃，并請駱駝。
At the end of the Zhenjun era, the emperor undertook a southern campaign and was about to advance on Pengcheng. Liu Yilong's son, the Prince of Wuling, Jun — who held the titles General Who Pacifies the North and Inspector of Xu Province — sent the general Ma Wengong with more than ten thousand infantry and cavalry to Xiaocheng. The vanguard routed them. Wengong fled and escaped, but his squad leader Kuai Ying was captured. When Yilong learned that the emperor was touring south, he also sent his younger brother, the Prince of Jiangxia, Yigong — who held the title Grand Commandant — with troops to Pengcheng. When Shizu reached Pengcheng, he climbed the mound of the Second Father to look into the city, sent Kuai Ying to the Lesser Market Gate, proclaimed the emperor's edict, conveyed greetings to Yigong and the others, [1] and had him describe the defeat at Xiaocheng. Yigong and the others asked Ying, "Has the Wei emperor come in person?" Ying replied, "He has come in person." They asked again, "Where is he now?" Ying replied, "Southwest of the city." They asked again, "How many troops and horses are there?" Ying replied, "The central army numbers more than four hundred thousand." Jun sent men to present two vessels of wine and a hundred stalks of sugarcane, and also to request camels.
5
世祖明旦復登亞父冢，遣孝伯至小市，駿亦遣其長史張暢對孝伯。 孝伯遙問暢姓，暢曰：「姓張。 」孝伯曰：「是張長史也。 」暢曰：「君何得見識？ 」孝伯曰：「既涉此境，何容不悉。 」暢問孝伯曰：「君復何姓？ 居何官也？ 」孝伯曰：「我戎行一夫，何足致問。 然足與君相敵。 」孝伯曰：「主上有詔：『太尉、安北可暫出門，欲與相見，朕亦不攻彭城，何為勞苦將士，城上嚴備？ 』今遣賜駱駝及貂裘雜物。 」暢曰：「有詔之言，政可施於彼國，何得稱之於此？ 」孝伯曰：「卿家太尉、安北，是人臣不？ 」暢曰：「是也。 」孝伯曰：「我朝廷奄有萬國，率土之濱，莫敢不臣，縱為隣國之君，何為不稱詔於隣國之臣？ 」孝伯又問暢曰：「何至忽遽杜門絕橋？ 」暢曰：「二王以魏帝壁壘未立，將士疲勞，此精甲十萬，人思致命，恐輕相凌踐，故且閉城耳。 待休息士馬，然後共治戰場，剋日交戲。 」孝伯曰：「令行禁止，主將常事，宜當以法裁物，何用發橋杜門？ 窮城之中，復何以十萬誇大？ 我亦有良馬百萬，復可以此相矜。 」暢曰：「王侯設險，何但法令而已也。 我若誇君，當言百萬，所以言十萬者，正是二王左右素所畜養者耳。 此城內有數州士庶，工徒營伍猶所未論。 我本鬬人，不鬬馬足。 且冀之北土，馬之所生，君復何以逸足見誇也？ 」孝伯曰：「王侯設險，誠如來言，開閉有常，何為杜塞？ 絕橋之意，義在何也？ 此城守君之所習，野戰我之所長，我之恃馬，猶如君之恃城耳。 」城內有貝思者，[2]嘗至京師，義恭遣視之，思識是孝伯。 思前問孝伯曰：「李尚書行途有勞。 」孝伯曰：「此事應相與共知。 」思答曰：「緣共知，所以仰勞。 」孝伯曰：「感君至意。」
The next morning Shizu again climbed the mound of the Second Father and sent Xiaobo to the Lesser Market. Jun also sent his Chief Clerk Zhang Chang to meet Xiaobo. From a distance Xiaobo asked Chang his surname. Chang said, "My surname is Zhang." Xiaobo said, "That must be Chief Clerk Zhang." Chang said, "How did you recognize me?" Xiaobo said, "Having entered this territory, how could I not know you?" Chang asked Xiaobo, "And what is your surname? What office do you hold?" Xiaobo said, "I am but one man in the army — hardly worth asking about. Yet I am quite your match." Xiaobo said, "The sovereign has an edict: 'Grand Commandant and General Who Pacifies the North may come outside the gate for a time; he wishes to meet you. I likewise shall not attack Pengcheng — so why trouble your officers and men with strict defenses on the walls?' He now sends camels, sable furs, and various goods as gifts.'" Chang said, "Language fit for an edict may be used in your state — how can it be invoked here?" Xiaobo said, "Are your Grand Commandant and General Who Pacifies the North subjects or not?" Chang said, "They are." Xiaobo said, "Our court embraces the myriad states; along the shores of the land none dares refuse submission. Even as sovereign of a neighboring state, why should he not speak by edict to subjects of a neighboring state?" Xiaobo further asked Chang, "Why go so far as to shut the gates and cut the bridges in such haste?" Chang said, "The two princes saw that the Wei emperor's encampments were not yet established and the troops were weary. Here are a hundred thousand elite armored men who all long to give their lives, and they feared a rash assault — so for the moment the city is closed." When horses and men have rested, we shall together set the battlefield and fix a day for battle." Xiaobo said, "Enforcing orders and prohibiting transgression is the constant duty of a commander-in-chief. One should measure affairs by law — what need is there to cut bridges and shut gates? Within a besieged city, how can one boast of a hundred thousand? We too have a million fine horses — shall we boast of that as well?" Chang said, "When lords and princes establish defenses, that is more than mere laws and regulations. If I were to boast to you, I would say a million. The reason I say a hundred thousand is precisely the men the two princes have long kept about them. Within this city are people from several provinces — craftsmen, laborers, and garrison troops are still uncounted. I came to fight men, not to compete in horses. Moreover the northern lands of Ji are where horses are bred — with what fleet steeds do you boast?" Xiaobo said, "Lords and princes establish defenses — truly as you say. Opening and closing have their rules — why block and seal everything? As for cutting the bridges — what is the point? Siege defense is what you excel at; field battle is what we excel at. Our reliance on horses is just like your reliance on walls." Within the city was one Bei Si, [2] who had once been to the capital. Yigong sent him to look, and Si recognized Xiaobo. Si stepped forward and said to Xiaobo, "Minister Li, the journey must have been wearying." Xiaobo said, "This matter ought to be known to us both." Si answered, "Because it is known to us both, I offer my respects for your labors." Xiaobo said, "I am moved by your courtesy."
6
既開門，暢屏人却仗，出受賜物。 孝伯曰：「詔以貂裘賜太尉，駱駝、騾、馬賜安北，蒲萄酒及諸食味當相與同進。 」暢曰：「二王敬白魏帝，知欲垂見，常願面接，但受命本朝，忝居藩任，人臣無境外之交，故無容私覿。 」義恭獻皮袴褶一具，駿奉酒二器、甘蔗百梃。 孝伯曰：「又有詔：『太尉、安北，久絕南信，殊當憂悒。 若欲遣信者，當為護送，脫須騎者，亦當以馬送之。 』」暢曰：「此方間路甚多，使命日夕往復，不復以此勞魏帝也。 」孝伯曰：「亦知有水路，似為白賊所斷。 」暢曰：「君著白衣，稱白賊也。 」孝伯大笑曰：「今之白賊，似異黃巾、赤眉。 」暢曰：「黃巾、赤眉，不在江南。 」孝伯曰：「雖不在江南，亦不離徐方也。 」孝伯曰：「向與安北相聞，何以久而不報？ 」暢曰：「二王貴遠，啟聞為難。 」孝伯曰：「周公握髮吐餔，二王何獨貴遠？ 」暢曰：「握髮吐餐，不謂隣國之人也。 」孝伯曰：「本邦尚爾，隣國彌應盡恭。 且賓至有禮，主人宜以禮接。 」暢曰：「昨見眾賓至門，未為有禮。 」孝伯曰：「非是賓至無禮，直是主人怱怱，無待賓調度耳。 」孝伯又言：「有詔：『程天祚一介常人，誠知非江南之選，近於汝陽，身被九槍，落在溵水，我使牽而出之。 凡人骨肉分張，並思集聚，聞其弟在此，如何不遣暫出？ 尋自令反，豈復苟留一人。 』」暢曰：「知欲程天祚兄弟集聚，已勒遣之，但其固辭不往。 」孝伯曰：「豈有子弟聞其父兄而反不肯相見，此便禽獸之不若。 貴土風俗，何至如此。」
Once the gate was opened, Chang dismissed his attendants, laid aside his weapons, came out, and received the gifts. Xiaobo said, "The edict bestows sable furs on the Grand Commandant and camels, mules, and horses on the General Who Pacifies the North. Grape wine and various delicacies are to be brought in together." Chang said, "The two princes respectfully inform the Wei emperor that, knowing he wishes to grant an audience, they have always desired a face-to-face meeting. But having received orders from their own court and holding feudal posts, subjects may have no dealings outside their borders — hence there can be no private audience." Yigong presented one set of leather trousers and jacket. Jun offered two vessels of wine and a hundred stalks of sugarcane. Xiaobo said, "There is also an edict: 'Grand Commandant and General Who Pacifies the North, long cut off from news from the south, must be deeply troubled. If you wish to send messengers, we shall escort them. Should you need riders, we shall likewise provide horses to deliver them.'" Chang said, "On this side there are many byways, and messengers come and go day and night — we need not further trouble the Wei emperor with this." Xiaobo said, "We know there is also a water route, but it seems to have been cut off by White Bandits." Chang said, "You wear white garments — you are the White Bandits." Xiaobo laughed heartily and said, "Today's White Bandits seem unlike the Yellow Turbans and Red Eyebrows." Chang said, "The Yellow Turbans and Red Eyebrows are not in Jiangnan." Xiaobo said, "Though not in Jiangnan, they are not far from the Xu region either." Xiaobo said, "Earlier I exchanged messages with the General Who Pacifies the North — why has there been no reply for so long?" Chang said, "The two princes are of lofty rank and far removed; reporting and inquiry are difficult." Xiaobo said, "The Duke of Zhou would clench his hair and spit out his food in haste — why alone should the two princes be so lofty and remote?" Chang said, "Clenching one's hair and spitting out one's food — that is not said of people of a neighboring state." Xiaobo said, "If even within one's own state it is so, toward a neighboring state one should all the more show full deference. Moreover, when guests arrive, the host ought to receive them with propriety." Chang said, "Yesterday I saw many guests reach the gate — that was hardly propriety." Xiaobo said, "It was not that the guests arrived without propriety — the host was simply in haste and did not wait to arrange for the guests." Xiaobo spoke again: "There is an edict: 'Cheng Tianzuo is an ordinary common man and truly no choice man of Jiangnan. Near Ruyang he took nine spear wounds and fell into the Yin River — I had him pulled out. Ordinary people, their flesh and bone scattered, all long to reunite. Hearing his younger brother is here, why not send him out briefly? Soon I shall let him return — how could I detain a single man wantonly?'" Chang said, "Knowing you wish the Cheng Tianzuo brothers to reunite, we have already ordered him sent, but he firmly refuses to go." Xiaobo said, "How can there be sons and younger brothers who, hearing of their father and elder brothers, yet refuse to meet? This is not even as good as birds and beasts. What customs of your noble land reach to such a point?"
7
世祖又遣賜義恭、駿等氈各一領，鹽各九種，并胡豉。 孝伯曰：「有後詔：『凡此諸鹽，各有所宜。 白鹽食鹽，主上自食； 黑鹽治腹脹氣滿，末之六銖，以酒而服； 胡鹽治目痛； 戎鹽治諸瘡； 赤鹽、駁鹽、臭鹽、馬齒鹽四種，並非食鹽。 太尉、安北何不遣人來至朕間？ 彼此之情，雖不可盡，要復見朕小大，知朕老少，觀朕為人。 』」暢曰：「魏帝久為往來所具，李尚書親自銜命，不患彼此不盡，故不復遣信。 」義恭獻蠟燭十梃，駿獻錦一匹。
Shizu again sent one rug each to Yigong, Jun, and the others, nine kinds of salt each, and fermented bean paste from the north. Xiaobo said, "There is a further edict: 'Each of these salts has its proper use. White salt and table salt the sovereign eats himself; black salt treats abdominal distension and fullness of qi — grind six zhu of it and take it with wine; Hu salt treats eye pain; barbarian salt treats various sores; red salt, variegated salt, foul salt, and horsetooth salt — these four kinds are none of them table salt. Grand Commandant and General Who Pacifies the North — why not send someone to my presence? Feelings between us, though they cannot be fully expressed, should at least let you see my stature, know my age, and observe what manner of man I am.'" Chang said, "The Wei emperor has long been fully described in our mutual exchanges. Minister Li himself bears the commission — we need not fear that feelings on both sides are not fully conveyed, hence we do not send a messenger again." Yigong presented ten candles. Jun presented one bolt of brocade.
8
孝伯曰：「君南土士人，何為著屩？ 君而著此，將士云何？ 」暢曰：「士人之言，誠為多愧。 但以不武，受命統軍，戎陳之間，不容緩服。 」孝伯曰：「永昌王自頃恒鎮長安，今領精騎八萬直造淮南，壽春亦閉門自固，不敢相禦。 向送劉康祖首，彼之所見。 王玄謨甚是所悉，亦是常才耳。 何意作如此任使，以致奔敗。 自入境七百餘里，主人竟不能一相拒抗。 鄒山之險，彼之所憑，前鋒始得接手，崔邪利便爾入穴，將士倒曳出之。 主上丐其生命，今從在此。 復何以輕脫，遣馬文恭至蕭縣，使望風退撓也。 彼之民人，甚相忿怨，言清平之時，賦我租帛，至有急難，不能相拯。 」暢曰：「知永昌已過淮南。 康祖為其所破，比有信使，無此消息。 王玄謨南土偏將，不謂為才，但以其北人，故為前驅引導耳。 大軍未至，而河冰向合，玄謨量宜反旆，未為失算，但因夜回歸，致戎馬驚亂耳。 我家懸瓠小城，陳憲小將，魏帝傾國攻圍，累旬不克。 胡盛之偏裨小帥，眾無三旅，始濟翮水，[3]魏國君臣奔散，僅得免脫。 滑臺之師，無所多愧。 鄒山小戍，雖有微險，河畔之民，多是新附，始慕政化，姦盜未息，示使崔邪利撫之而已。 [4]今雖陷沒，何損於國。 魏帝自以十萬之師而制一崔邪利，乃復足言也？ 近聞蕭縣百姓並依山險，聊遣馬文恭以十隊迎之耳。 文恭前以三隊出，還走彼大營。 嵇玄敬以百舸至留城，魏軍奔敗。 輕敵致此，亦非所卹。 王境人民，列居河畔，二國交兵，當互加撫養。 而魏師入境，事生意外，官不負民，民亦何怨。 知入境七百里，無相捍拒，此自上由太尉神算，次在武陵聖略，軍國之要，雖不預聞，然用兵有機間，亦不容相語。 」孝伯曰：「君藉此虛談，支離相對，可謂遁辭知其所窮。 且主上當不圍此城，自率眾軍直造瓜步。 南事若辦，城故不待攻圍； 南行不捷，彭城亦非所欲也。 我今當南，欲飲馬江湖耳。 」暢曰：「去留之事，自適彼懷。 若魏帝遂得飲馬長江，便為無復天道。 」孝伯曰：「自北而南，實惟人化，飲馬長江，豈獨天道？ 」暢將還城，謂孝伯曰：「冀蕩定有期，相見無遠。 君若得還宋朝，今為相識之始。 」孝伯曰：「今當先至建業以待君耳。 恐爾日君與二王面縛請罪，不暇為容。」
Xiaobo said, "You are a gentleman of the southern lands — why wear slippers? If you wear these, what shall the officers and men do?" Chang said, "Your words as a gentleman do indeed cause much shame. But being no warrior, yet having received orders to command armies, amid the battle array one cannot dress at ease." Xiaobo said, "The Prince of Yongchang has long garrisoned Chang'an. Now he leads eighty thousand elite cavalry straight toward Huainan. Shouyang too has shut its gates and holds firm, not daring to oppose. Recently we sent Liu Kangzu's head — that is what they have seen. Wang Xuanmo is very well known to us — he too is merely ordinary talent. Why appoint him to such a role as to end in flight and defeat? Since entering your territory more than seven hundred li, the host has not once been able to resist. The peril of Mount Zou was their reliance. Scarcely had the vanguard joined battle when Cui Xieli went straight into a cave, and the officers and men dragged him out headlong. The sovereign spared his life, and now he follows us here. Why again so lightly send Ma Wengong to Xiaoxian, causing him to falter and withdraw at sight of the enemy? The people there are deeply resentful, saying that in times of peace you levied their rents and cloth, yet when crisis came you could not save them." Chang said, "We know Yongchang has already passed Huainan. Kangzu was defeated by him, but according to recent messengers there is no such news. Wang Xuanmo is a partial general of the southern lands — not counted as talented, but because he is a northerner he was made vanguard and guide. The great army had not yet arrived and the river ice was about to close. Xuanmo judged it fit to turn back — that was no miscalculation, but the night retreat caused horses and troops to panic and scatter. Our little town of Xuanhuo — the minor general Chen Xian — the Wei emperor threw the whole state's force against it in siege for many weeks without taking it. Hu Shengzhi, a petty subordinate commander with fewer than three regiments, had just crossed the Yi River [3] when the Wei state's lords and ministers scattered in flight and barely escaped. As for the army at Huatai — there is little to be ashamed of. The little fort at Mount Zou, though it had slight strategic advantage, had riverside people mostly newly submitted, just beginning to admire civilized rule while theft and banditry had not ceased — they merely sent Cui Xieli to pacify them. [4] Though it has now fallen, what loss is that to the state? The Wei emperor himself needed a hundred-thousand-man army to take one Cui Xieli — is that even worth mentioning? Recently we heard the people of Xiaoxian all cling to mountain defiles — we merely sent Ma Wengong with ten squads to receive them. Wengong earlier went out with three squads and returned fleeing to their great camp. Ji Xuanjing with a hundred ships reached Liucheng — the Wei army fled in defeat. Contempt for the enemy brought this — it is not what we regret. The people of the royal domains dwell along the river — when two states clash in arms, each side ought to extend mutual care. But when the Wei army entered the territory, matters arose beyond expectation. The officials did not fail the people — why should the people resent? Knowing you penetrated seven hundred li without meeting resistance — this from above rests on the Grand Commandant's divine calculation, next on the Prince of Wuling's sagely strategy. The essentials of army and state, though not heard in advance, yet in employing troops there are secret designs that cannot be shared." Xiaobo said, "You rely on this empty talk, matching me with fractured replies — one may call it evasive speech that shows where you are cornered. Moreover the sovereign will not besiege this city. He will himself lead the hosts straight to Guabu. If affairs in the south succeed, the city naturally need not await siege; if the southern advance is not victorious, Pengcheng is not what he desires either. I now go south — I mean only to water my horses in the rivers and lakes." Chang said, "Matters of going and staying suit your own wish. If the Wei emperor should truly water his horses in the Yangtze, that would mean Heaven's Way no longer exists." Xiaobo said, "From north to south is truly human transformation. Watering horses in the Yangtze — is that solely Heaven's Way?" As Chang was about to return to the city, he said to Xiaobo, "I hope pacification will come in due time. Our meeting again will not be far off. If you should return to the Song court, today is the beginning of our acquaintance." Xiaobo said, "I shall now go first to Jiankang to await you. I fear that day you and the two princes will be bound facing forward to beg pardon, with no leisure for pleasantries."
9
孝伯風容閑雅，應答如流，暢及左右甚相嗟歎。 世祖大喜，進爵宣城公。
Xiaobo's bearing was leisurely and refined, his replies fluent as a stream. Chang and those beside him greatly sighed in admiration. Shizu was greatly pleased and advanced his noble rank to Duke of Xuancheng.
10
興安二年，出為使持節、散騎常侍、平西將軍、秦州刺史。 [5]太安五年卒，高宗甚悼惜之。 贈鎮南大將軍、定州刺史，諡曰文昭公。
In the second year of Xing'an he was sent out as Bearer of the Staff of Authority, Regular Attendant, General Who Pacifies the West, and Inspector of Qin Province. [5] In the fifth year of Tai'an he died. Emperor Gaozong deeply mourned and grieved for him. He was posthumously appointed Grand General Who Guards the South and Inspector of Ding Province, and given the posthumous name Duke Wen Zhao.
11
孝伯體度恢雅，明達政事，朝野貴賤，咸推重之。 恭宗曾啟世祖廣徵俊秀，世祖曰：「朕有一孝伯，足治天下，何用多為？ 假復求訪，此人輩亦何可得。 」其見賞如此。 性方慎忠厚，每朝廷大事有不足，必手自書表，切言陳諫，或不從者，至於再三。 削滅稿草，家人不見。 公庭論議，常引綱紀，或有言事者，孝伯恣其所陳，假有是非，終不抑折。 及見世祖，言其所長，初不隱人姓名以為己善，故衣冠之士，服其雅正。 自崔浩誅後，軍國之謀，咸出孝伯。 世祖寵眷有亞於浩，亦以宰輔遇之。 獻替補闕，其迹不見，時人莫得而知也。 卒之日，遠近哀傷焉。 孝伯美名，聞於遐邇，李彪使於江南，蕭賾謂之曰：「孝伯於卿遠近？ 」其為遠人所知若此。 孝伯妻崔賾女，高明婦人，生一子元顯。 崔氏卒後，納翟氏，不以為妻也。 憎忌元顯。 後遇劫，元顯見害，世云翟氏所為也。 元顯志氣甚高，為時人所傷惜。 翟氏二子，安民、安上，並有風度。
Xiaobo's stature and manner were magnanimous and refined. He was clear and penetrating in governance, and nobles and commoners, court and country, all esteemed him. Emperor Gongzong once urged Shizu to broadly summon outstanding talent. Shizu said, "I have one Xiaobo — enough to govern the realm. Why need many? Even if one sought them out, men of this sort — how could they be obtained?" Such was the esteem in which he was held. By nature he was upright, cautious, and loyal. Whenever great affairs of court fell short, he necessarily wrote memorials in his own hand and spoke forthrightly in remonstrance. If not heeded, he would do so twice and thrice. He destroyed draft copies, and his family did not see them. In court discussion he always invoked fundamental principles. When someone spoke on affairs, Xiaobo let them state all they wished. Even if there were right and wrong, he never suppressed or cut short. When he saw Shizu, he spoke of others' strengths. He never concealed people's names to claim credit for himself — hence the gentry admired his refined integrity. After Cui Hao was executed, military and state counsel all issued from Xiaobo. Shizu's favor toward him was second only to Hao's, and he was also treated as a chief minister. His counsel in reform and his rectification of omissions left no visible trace, and people of the time could not know them. On the day he died, far and near grieved. Xiaobo's fine reputation was heard in distant regions. When Li Biao was envoy to Jiangnan, Xiao Ze said to him, "Is Xiaobo far from you or near?" Such was the extent to which distant people knew of him. Xiaobo's wife was a daughter of Cui Zhen, a capable woman. She bore one son, Yuan Xian. After the Lady Cui died, he took the Lady Zhai but did not make her his wife. She hated and envied Yuan Xian. Later, during a robbery, Yuan Xian was killed. The world said it was the work of the Lady Zhai. Yuan Xian's spirit and resolve were very lofty, and people of the time mourned and grieved for him. The Lady Zhai's two sons, Anmin and Anshang, both had fine bearing.
12
安民，襲爵壽光侯，司徒司馬。 卒，贈郢州刺史。 無子，爵除。
Anmin inherited the marquisate of Shouguang and served as Chief Clerk of the Ministry of Education. When he died, he was posthumously appointed Inspector of Ying Province. He had no son, and the noble rank was extinguished.
13
安上，鉅鹿太守，亦早卒。
Anshang was Administrator of Julu and also died young.
14
安民弟豹子。 正光三年上書曰：
Anmin's younger brother was Baozi. In the third year of Zhengguang he submitted a memorial saying:
15
竊惟庸勳賞勞，有國恒典； 興滅繼絕，哲后所先。 是以積德累忠，春秋許宥十世； 立功著節，河山誓其永久。 伏惟世祖太武皇帝，英叡自天，籠罩日域，東清遼海，西定玉門，凌滅漠北，飲馬江水。 臣亡父故尚書、宣城公先臣孝伯，冥基感會，邀幸昌辰，綢繆幃幄，繾綣侍從，廟算嘉謀、每蒙顧採。 于時儲后監國，奏請徵賢，詔報曰：「朕有一孝伯，足以治天下，何用多為？ 」其見委遇，乃至於此。 是用寵以元、凱，爵以公侯，詔冊曰：「江陽之巡，奇謀屢進，六師大捷，亦有勳焉。 」出內勤王，寵遇隆厚，方開大賞，而世祖登遐。 梓宮始遷，外任名岳。 高宗沖年纂運，未及追敍。
I reflect that rewarding meritorious service is the constant precedent of a state; reviving what is extinguished and continuing what is broken off is what a sage sovereign puts first. Thus it is that when virtue is heaped up and loyalty accumulated, the Spring and Autumn Annals permitted grace to extend across ten generations; when merit was won and integrity made manifest, the rivers and mountains themselves were sworn to preserve the reward forever. I humbly reflect that Emperor Shizu the Grand Martial Emperor, with sage brilliance granted by Heaven, cast his shadow over the entire realm: he cleared the eastern seas, secured the Jade Gate in the west, swept the northern deserts, and watered his horses at the Yangtze. My late father, the former Minister of Works and Duke of Xuancheng, your subject Xiaobo, was drawn by hidden merit and fortunate timing into an age of glory. He served close within the imperial curtain, intimate in attendance; whenever plans were weighed in the temple, his counsel was chosen again and again. At that time the crown prince was regent and memorialized the throne to summon men of talent. The imperial reply came: "I already have Xiaobo—he is enough to govern the realm. Why summon more?" Such was the depth of the trust and favor shown him. For this he was honored with the highest ministerial rank and ennobled a duke or marquis. The patent read: "On the Jiangyang expedition his ingenious plans were offered again and again; in the great triumph of the six armies he too had a share of the achievement." Within the palace and beyond it he served the throne with tireless loyalty, and the honors heaped upon him were great. Just as a grand reward was about to be granted, Emperor Shizu departed this life. When the imperial coffin was first borne away, he was posted to a distinguished frontier commandery. Emperor Gaozong came to the throne in his youth and had not yet had occasion to grant retrospective honors.
16
臣行舛百靈，先臣棄世，微績未甄，誠志長奪，搢紳僉傷早世，朝野咸哀不永。 臣亡兄襲，無子封除。 永惟宗構，五情崩圮。 先臣榮寵前朝，勳書王府，同之常倫，爵封堙墜，準古量今，實深荼苦。 竊惟朝例：廣川王遵、太原公元大曹等，並以勳重先朝，世絕繼祀，或以傍親，或聽弟襲，皆傳河山之功，垂不世之賞。 況先臣在蒙委任，[6]運籌幃帟，勳著於中，聲傳於外。 事等功均，今古無易。 是以漢賞信布，裁重良平； 魏酬張徐，不棄荀郭。 今數族追賞於先朝之世，先臣絕封於聖明之時，瞻流顧侶，存亡永恨。 竊見正始中，爰發存亡之詔，褒賢報功之旨。 熙平元年，故任城王澄所請十事，復新前澤，成一時之盛事，垂曠代之茂典，凡在纓紱，誰不感慶？ 蓋以奬勸來今，垂範萬古。 且劉氏偽書，翻流上國，尋其訕謗，百無一實，前後使人，不書姓字，亦無名爵。 至於張暢傳中，略敍先臣對問，雖改脫略盡，自欲矜高，然逸韻難虧，猶見稱載，非直存益於時，沒亦有彰國美。 乞覽此書，昭然可見。 則微微衰構，重起一朝，先臣潛魂，結草於千載矣。
My own life has gone astray before heaven and earth; my late father has left the world; his modest achievements were never fully recognized, his earnest devotion cut short forever. The gentry grieved that he died too soon; court and countryside alike mourned that his years were too few. My late elder brother Xi succeeded to the title, but left no son, and the enfeoffment was abolished. When I think forever on the ancestral line, all five emotions within me crumble like a wall. My late father was honored in the previous reign and his deeds were entered in the royal archives; yet by ordinary rule his rank and fief have sunk into oblivion. Measured against ancient precedent and weighed against our own age, the bitterness is truly unbearable. I have reviewed the court's precedents: Prince Guangchuan Zun, Yuantuogong Yuanda Cao, and others, because their merit in the former dynasty was great and their line ended with no heir to the sacrifices, were allowed succession through collateral kin or through younger brothers—all preserving the achievement sworn by river and mountain, and passing down rewards unmatched in their age. How much more so in the case of my late father, who was entrusted with command, [6] plotted strategy within the command tent, whose merit was manifest at court and whose fame resounded abroad! The deeds were equal and the merit comparable; from antiquity to the present the principle has not changed. Thus Han rewarded Han Xin and Ying Bu with honors as weighty as those given Liang and Ping; Wei repaid Zhang and Xu and did not cast aside Xun and Guo. Now other clans receive retrospective honors from the age of the former dynasty, while my late father's fief is extinguished in this sage reign. Looking to those who shared his path and turning to his peers, the living and the dead alike are left with everlasting regret. I have seen that in the Zhengshi era an edict was issued touching the living and the dead alike, with the intent of honoring the worthy and repaying merit. In the first year of Xiping, the ten petitions of the former Prince of Rencheng Cheng revived former grace, creating a great event of the age and a splendid statute for generations to come. Who among those girded with cap and sash did not rejoice? Surely this was meant to encourage those yet to come and to hand down a model for ten thousand ages. Moreover, the spurious history of the Liu clan circulates in our realm. Examine its slanders and not one claim in a hundred is true. Its envoys, past and present, give neither surname nor given name, nor any official title. In Zhang Chang's biography, my late father's replies at court are briefly recorded. Though the text has been altered and pared away almost to nothing, and though Zhang sought to elevate himself, the lingering force of the exchange cannot be erased; he is still cited with praise. This not only benefited the age while my father lived, but even after death brought glory to the state. I beg Your Majesty to read that book—the truth is plain to see. Then this faintly failing line would rise again in a single reign, and my late father's hidden spirit would repay the debt with tied grass a thousand years hence!
17
卒不得襲。
In the end the petition was denied and the line was not restored.
18
孝伯兄祥，字元善。 學傳家業，鄉黨宗之。 世祖詔州郡舉賢良，祥應貢，對策合旨，除中書博士。 時南土未賓，世祖親駕，遣尚書韓元興率眾出青州，以祥為軍司。 略地至于陳汝，淮北之民詣軍降者七千餘戶，遷之於兗豫之南，置淮陽郡以撫之，拜祥為太守，加綏遠將軍，流民歸之者萬餘家，勸課農桑，百姓安業。 世祖嘉之，賜以衣馬。 遷河間太守，有威恩之稱。 太安中，徵拜中書侍郎，民有千餘，上書乞留數年，高宗不許。 卒官，追贈定州刺史、平棘子，諡曰憲。
Xiaobo's elder brother Xiang, whose courtesy name was Yuanshan. He inherited the family tradition of scholarship, and his village and clan held him in esteem. When Emperor Shizu ordered the provinces and commanderies to recommend worthy and upright men, Xiang presented himself. His written answers accorded with the court's intent, and he was appointed Erudite of the Palace Library. At that time the south had not yet submitted. Emperor Shizu led the campaign in person and dispatched Minister of Works Han Yuanying with an army from Qing Province, appointing Xiang army aide. He advanced as far as Chen and Ru. More than seven thousand households north of the Huai came to the army and surrendered; they were resettled south of Yan and Yu, and Huaiyang Commandery was established to settle them. Xiang was made governor and given the additional title General Pacifying the Distance. More than ten thousand refugee households returned; he encouraged farming and sericulture, and the people lived in peace. Emperor Shizu praised him and bestowed robes and horses. He was transferred to Governor of Hejian, where he won a reputation for combining authority with kindness. In the Tai'an era he was summoned to the post of Palace Attendant. More than a thousand people submitted a memorial asking that he be kept several years longer, but Emperor Gaozong did not agree. He died in office. Posthumously he was ennobled Governor of Ding Province and Baron of Pingji, with the posthumous name Constitutional.
19
子安世，[7]幼而聰悟。 興安二年，高宗引見侍郎、博士之子，簡其秀儁者欲為中書學生。 安世年十一，高宗見其尚小，引問之。 安世陳說父祖，甚有次第，即以為學生。 高宗每幸國學，恒獨被引問。 詔曰：「汝但守此至大，不慮不富貴。 」居父憂以孝聞。 天安初，拜中散，以溫敏敬慎，顯祖親愛之。 累遷主客令。
His son Anshi [7] was clever and quick-witted from childhood. In the second year of Xing'an, Emperor Gaozong summoned the sons of Palace Attendants and Erudites and chose the most gifted among them to become students of the Palace Library. Anshi was eleven. Emperor Gaozong thought him still too young and called him forward to question him. Anshi described his father and ancestors in excellent order and was immediately enrolled as a student. Whenever Emperor Gaozong visited the National University, Anshi alone was always singled out for questioning. The emperor said: "Hold fast to this supreme talent, and you need never fear that wealth and rank will not come." During mourning for his father he became known for filial devotion. At the beginning of the Tian'an era he was appointed Palace Cadet. Warm, quick, respectful, and careful, he won the special favor of Emperor Xianzu. He rose through repeated promotions to Director of Guests.
20
蕭賾使劉纘朝貢，安世美容貌，善舉止，纘等自相謂曰：「不有君子，其能國乎？ 」纘等呼安世為典客，安世曰：「三代不共禮，五帝各異樂，安足以亡秦之官，稱於上國。 」纘曰：「世異之號，凡有幾也？ 」安世曰：「周謂掌客，秦改典客，漢名鴻臚，今曰主客。 君等不欲影響文武，而殷勤亡秦。 」纘又指方山曰：「此山去燕然遠近？ 」安世曰：「亦由石頭之於番禺耳。 」國家有江南使至，多出藏內珍物，令都下富室好容服者貨之，令使任情交易。 使至金玉肆問價，纘曰：「北方金玉大賤，當是山川所出？ 」安世曰：「聖朝不貴金玉，所以賤同瓦礫。 又皇上德通神明，山不愛寶，故無川無金，無山無玉。 」纘初將大市，得安世言，慚而罷。 遷主客給事中。
When Xiao Ze sent Liu Zuan to pay tribute at court, Anshi had a handsome face and graceful bearing. Zuan and his companions said to one another, "Without such gentlemen, how could a state endure?" " Zuan and the others addressed Anshi as "Director of Ceremonies." Anshi replied, "The Three Dynasties did not share one ritual code; the Five Emperors each had different music. How can a title from the fallen Qin be used to address an envoy of a superior state?" " Zuan asked, "How many such titles have changed with the ages?" " Anshi said, "Zhou called the office Director of Guests; Qin changed it to Director of Ceremonies; Han named it Grand Master of Ceremonies; today it is Director of Guests." "You are unwilling to invoke the Zhou of King Wen and King Wu, yet so eager to borrow a Qin title from a fallen dynasty." " Zuan also pointed to Mount Fang and asked, "How far is this mountain from Yanran?" " Anshi replied, "About as far as Mount Stone is from Panyu." When envoys arrived from the south, the court often brought out rare goods from the palace stores and had wealthy men of the capital who loved fine dress buy them up, letting the envoys trade as they wished. When the envoys came to a gold and jade market to ask prices, Zuan said, "Gold and jade are very cheap in the north. Surely they must come from your mountains and rivers?" " Anshi said, "Our sage dynasty does not prize gold and jade, and so they are valued no higher than tiles and rubble." "Moreover the Emperor's virtue reaches to the spirits; the mountains do not hoard their treasures. Thus there is no river without gold and no hill without jade." At first Zuan meant to buy heavily, but after hearing Anshi he was ashamed and gave it up. He was promoted to Director of Guests and Supervising Censor.
21
時民困飢流散，豪右多有占奪，安世乃上疏曰：「臣聞量地畫野，經國大式； 邑地相參，致治之本。 井稅之興，其來日久； 田萊之數，制之以限。 蓋欲使土不曠功，民罔游力。 雄擅之家，不獨膏腴之美； 單陋之夫，亦有頃畝之分。 所以恤彼貧微，抑茲貪欲，同富約之不均，一齊民於編戶。 竊見州郡之民，或因年儉流移，棄賣田宅，漂居異鄉，事涉數世。 三長既立，[8]始返舊墟，廬井荒毀，桑榆改植。 事已歷遠，易生假冒。 強宗豪族，肆其侵凌，遠認魏晉之家，近引親舊之驗。 又年載稍久，鄉老所惑，羣證雖多，莫可取據。 各附親知，互有長短，兩證徒具，聽者猶疑，爭訟遷延，連紀不判。 良疇委而不開，柔桑枯而不採，僥倖之徒興，繁多之獄作。 欲令家豐歲儲，人給資用，其可得乎！ 愚謂今雖桑井難復，宜更均量，審其徑術，令分藝有準，力業相稱，細民獲資生之利，豪右靡餘地之盈。 則無私之澤，乃播均於兆庶； 如阜如山，可有積於比戶矣。 又所爭之田，宜限年斷，事久難明，悉屬今主。 然後虛妄之民，絕望於覬覦； 守分之士，永免於凌奪矣。 」高祖深納之，後均田之制起於此矣。
At that time the people suffered famine and drifted away in flight, and powerful families often seized land by force. Anshi submitted a memorial: "I have heard that measuring land and marking out the realm is the great pattern by which a state is governed; matching settlements to territory is the foundation of good government. The well-field tax arose long ago; and the extent of cultivated and fallow land was fixed by limit. The aim was to keep the soil from lying idle and the people from wasting their strength. Great predatory houses did not monopolize all the richest land alone; poor and humble men also had their measure of acres. Thus the poor were sheltered, greed restrained, the imbalance of plenty and want corrected, and the common people brought together as one under the registers. I have observed that in the provinces and commanderies, when years were lean people drifted away, abandoning and selling fields and houses, settling in distant places, until the matter stretched over several generations. After the three-chiefs system was established, [8] people began returning to old homesteads, but houses and wells lay in ruins and mulberry and elm trees had been replanted elsewhere. Because so much time had passed, false claims were easily made. Powerful clans and great families encroached at will, citing distant Wei and Jin households in the far past and recent kin and old ties as proof. As the years lengthened, village elders were bewildered; though witnesses were many, none could serve as reliable proof. Each party rallied kin and acquaintances, contradicting one another. Two sets of testimony might be complete, yet the judges still hesitated; lawsuits dragged on for years without resolution. Good fields lay untilled, tender mulberry withered unharvested; opportunists flourished and lawsuits multiplied. If the aim is for every household to store grain and every person to have what he needs, how can that be achieved? I submit that although the old mulberry-and-well system cannot easily be restored, land should be reassessed and reallocated by clear measure, so that holdings have a standard, labor matches occupation, common people gain a livelihood, and powerful families have no surplus land to hoard. Then impartial bounty would reach evenly to the multitude; and like hills heaped high, plenty could accumulate in every household. Disputed fields, moreover, should be settled by a time limit: what has long been unclear should belong to the present owner. Then the false and grasping would lose hope of seizure; and those who kept to their proper share would forever be safe from seizure." Emperor Gaozu accepted this deeply. From this arose the equal-field system.
22
出為安平將軍、相州刺史、假節、趙郡公。 敦勸農桑，禁斷淫祀。 西門豹、史起，有功於民者，為之修飾廟堂。 表薦廣平宋翻、陽平路恃慶，皆為朝廷善士。 初，廣平人李波，宗族強盛，殘掠生民。 前刺史薛道𢷋親往討之，波率其宗族拒戰，大破𢷋軍。 遂為逋逃之藪，公私成患。 百姓為之語曰：「李波小妹字雍容，褰裙逐馬如卷蓬，左射右射必疊雙。 婦女尚如此，男子那可逢！ 」安世設方略誘波及諸子姪三十餘人，斬于鄴市，境內肅然。 以病免。 太和十七年卒于家。 安世妻博陵崔氏，生一子瑒。 崔氏以妬悍見出，又尚滄水公主，生二子，謐、郁。
He was sent out as General of Anping, Governor of Xiang Province, with provisional insignia, and ennobled Duke of Zhao Commandery. He earnestly encouraged farming and sericulture and banned improper cults. For Ximen Bao and Shi Qi, who had served the people well, he restored and adorned their temple halls. He recommended Song Fan of Guangping and Lu Shiqing of Yangping, both worthy men of the court. Earlier, a man of Guangping named Li Bo had a powerful clan that preyed upon the people. The previous governor Xue Daozhen went in person to suppress him. Bo rallied his clan to fight and routed Daozhen's army. Thereafter the place became a refuge for fugitives and a plague to public and private interests alike. The people had a saying: "Li Bo's little sister, called Yongrong, lifts her skirt and rides after horses like rolling tumbleweed; whether she shoots left or right she always brings down a pair." "If the women are like this, what hope have you against the men!" Anshi devised a plan to lure Bo and more than thirty of his sons and nephews, and had them beheaded in the market at Ye. Thereafter the region was quiet. He resigned on grounds of illness. In the seventeenth year of Taihe he died at home. Anshi's wife was Lady Cui of Boling, who bore one son, Yang. Lady Cui was cast out for jealousy and harsh temper. He then married the Princess of Cangshui and had two sons, Mi and Yu.

瑒，字琚羅。 涉歷史傳，頗有文才，氣尚豪爽，公強當世。 延昌末，司徒行參軍，遷司徒長兼主簿。 太師、高陽王雍表薦瑒為其友，正主簿。
Yang, whose courtesy name was Jurou. He read widely in history and had real literary talent. Bold and open in spirit, he stood forthright in his age. At the end of the Yanxi era he served as Aide in the Department of State Affairs, then was transferred to Senior Clerk and concurrently Chief Clerk. 于時民多絕戶而為沙門，瑒上言：「禮以教世，法導將來，跡用既殊，區流亦別。 故三千之罪，莫大不孝，不孝之大，無過於絕祀。 然則絕祀之罪，重莫甚焉。 安得輕縱背禮之情，而肆其向法之意也？ 正使佛道，亦不應然，假令聽然，猶須裁之以禮。 一身親老，棄家絕養，既非人理，尤乖禮情，堙滅大倫，且闕王貫。 交缺當世之禮，而求將來之益，孔子云『未知生，焉知死』，斯言之至，亦為備矣。 安有棄堂堂之政，而從鬼教乎！ 又今南服未靜，眾役仍煩，百姓之情，方多避役。 若復聽之，恐捐棄孝慈，比屋而是。 」沙門都統僧暹等忿瑒鬼教之言，以瑒為謗毀佛法，泣訴靈太后，太后責之。 瑒自理曰：「竊欲清明佛法，使道俗兼通，非敢排棄真學，妄為訾毀。 且鬼神之名，皆通靈達稱，自百代正典，敍三皇五帝，皆號為鬼。 天地曰神祇，人死曰鬼。 易曰『知鬼神之情狀』，周公自美，亦云『能事鬼神』，禮曰『明則有禮樂，幽則有鬼神』。 是以明者為堂堂，幽者為鬼教。 佛非天非地，本出於人，應世導俗，其道幽隱，名之為鬼，愚謂非謗。 且心無不善，以佛道為教者，正可未達眾妙之門耳。 」靈太后雖知瑒言為允，然不免暹等之意，猶罰瑒金一兩。 [9]
At that time many people abandoned their households to become monks. Yang submitted a memorial: "Rites instruct the age and law guides the future. Because their purposes differ, their spheres must be kept apart. Among the three thousand offenses, none is greater than lack of filial piety; and among forms of filial failure, none is worse than cutting off the ancestral sacrifices. The offense of extinguishing the sacrifices, then, could hardly be graver. How then can one lightly indulge feelings that violate ritual and freely indulge intentions that flee into the law?" "Even on Buddhist grounds this should not be permitted; even if it were allowed, it would still have to be restrained by ritual. To leave aged parents, abandon home, and cut off support is already against human reason and doubly against ritual propriety. It destroys the great human bonds and severs the thread of royal order. One casts aside the rites of this life to seek profit in the life to come. Confucius said, "If you do not yet understand life, how can you understand death?" That saying, taken to its depth, says all that need be said. How can one abandon the bright governance of the court and follow a ghostly teaching?" "Moreover the south is not yet pacified and labor service remains heavy. Among the people the urge to evade corvée is already strong. If this were permitted again, I fear filial kindness would be cast aside in household after household." The Chief of Monks Sengxian and others, angered by Yang's talk of "ghost teaching," accused him of slandering the Buddhist Law. Weeping, they appealed to Empress Dowager Ling, and the empress dowager rebuked Yang. Yang replied in his own defense: "I wished only to clarify the Buddhist Law so that clergy and laity might understand one another. I did not dare reject true learning or recklessly slander it. Besides, the names of ghosts and spirits all refer to beings that reach the numinous realm. From the orthodox classics of a hundred generations, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors are all called ghosts. Heaven and earth are called spirits; the dead are called ghosts. The Changes says, "Know the nature of ghosts and spirits"; the Duke of Zhou praised himself by saying, "Able to serve ghosts and spirits"; the Rites say, "What is bright has rites and music; what is dark has ghosts and spirits." Thus what is bright is called the hall, and what is dark is called ghost teaching. The Buddha is neither heaven nor earth. He arose from mankind, responding to the age and guiding custom. His way is hidden and obscure, and to call it ghost teaching is, I submit, no slander. And if the heart is not without goodness, those who take Buddhism as their teaching may simply not yet have entered the gate of its deepest mysteries." Although Empress Dowager Ling knew Yang's argument was sound, she could not disregard Sengxian and the others; she still fined Yang one liang of gold. The text is deficient.

轉尚書郎，加伏波將軍。 隨蕭寶夤西征，以瑒為統軍，假寧遠將軍。 瑒德洽鄉閭，招募雄勇，其樂從者數百騎，瑒傾家賑恤，率之西討。 寶夤見瑒至，乃拊瑒肩曰：「子遠來，吾事辦矣。 」故其下每有戰功，軍中號曰「李公騎」。 寶夤又啟瑒為左丞，仍為別將，軍機戎政，皆與參決。 寶夤又啟為中書侍郎。 還朝，除鎮遠將軍、岐州刺史，坐辭不赴任免官。 建義初，於河陰遇害，時年四十五。 初贈鎮東將軍、尚書右僕射、殷州刺史，太昌中重贈散騎常侍、驃騎大將軍、儀同三司、冀州刺史。
He was transferred to Gentleman of the Secretariat and given the additional title General Who Calms the Waves. When he followed Xiao Baoyin on the western expedition, Yang was made army commander and given the provisional title General of Pacifying the Distance. Yang was trusted in his home district. He recruited bold warriors, and several hundred horsemen gladly followed. He spent his family fortune to support them and led them west on campaign. When Baoyin saw Yang arrive, he clapped his shoulder and said, "You have come from far away—my task is accomplished." After that, whenever his men won distinction in battle, the army called them "Lord Li's Horsemen." Baoyin also memorialized to appoint Yang Left Director while keeping him as a separate commander. Military affairs and frontier administration were all decided with his counsel. Baoyin again memorialized to appoint him Palace Attendant. On returning to court he was appointed General of Pacifying the Distance and Governor of Qi Province, but because he declined the post he was dismissed from office. At the beginning of Jianyi he was killed at Heyin, aged forty-five. Initially he was posthumously ennobled General of Pacifying the East, Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Governor of Yin Province. In the Taichang era he was again posthumously ennobled Palace Attendant, Grand General of Fast Cavalry, Equal in Honor to the Three Dukes, and Governor of Ji Province.

瑒俶儻有大志，好飲酒，篤於親知，每謂弟郁曰：「士大夫學問，稽博古今而罷，何用專經為老博士也？ 」與弟謐特相友愛，謐在鄉物故，瑒慟哭絕氣，久而方蘇，不食數日，期年之中，[10]形骸毀悴。 人倫哀歎之。 瑒三子。
Yang was unconventional and ambitious, fond of wine and deeply loyal to kin and friends. He often told his younger brother Yu, "A gentleman's learning should range broadly through past and present—that is enough. Why bury yourself in the classics and become an old pedant?" He was especially close to his younger brother Mi. When Mi died at home, Yang wailed until he stopped breathing and only slowly revived. He ate nothing for days, and within a year [10] he was wasted to skin and bone. All who knew them mourned this bond of brotherhood. Yang had three sons.

長子義盛，武定中，司徒倉曹參軍。
The eldest son Yisheng, in the Wuding era, served as Aide in the Granary Section of the Department of State Affairs.

瑒弟謐，字永和。 在逸士傳。
Yang's younger brother Mi, whose courtesy name was Yonghe. His biography appears among the Recluses.

謐弟郁，字永穆。 好學沉靜，博通經史。 自著作佐郎為廣平王懷友，懷深相禮遇。 時學士徐遵明教授山東，生徒甚盛，懷徵遵明在館，令郁問其五經義例十餘條，遵明所答數條而已。 稍遷國子博士。 自國學之建，諸博士率不講說，朝夕教授，惟郁而已。 謙虛雅寬，甚有儒者之風。 遷廷尉少卿，加冠軍將軍，轉通直散騎常侍。 建義中，以兄瑒卒，遂撫育孤姪，歸於鄉里。 永熙初，除散騎常侍、大將軍、[11]左光祿大夫、兼都官尚書，尋領給事黃門侍郎。 三年春，於顯陽殿講禮，詔郁執經，解說不窮，羣難鋒起，無廢談笑。 出帝及諸王公凡預聽者，莫不嗟善。 尋病卒，贈散騎常侍、都督定冀相滄殷五州軍事、驃騎大將軍、尚書左僕射、儀同三司、定州刺史。
Mi's younger brother Yu, whose courtesy name was Yongmu. Fond of learning and calm in temperament, he was broadly versed in the classics and histories. From Associate Author he became companion to Prince Huai of Guangping, who treated him with exceptional courtesy. At that time the scholar Xu Zunming taught in Shandong and had a great following. Huai summoned Zunming to his residence and had Yu question him on more than ten points of meaning and usage in the Five Classics; Zunming answered only a few. He was gradually promoted to Erudite of the National University. Since the founding of the National University, the erudites generally did not lecture; Yu alone taught morning and evening. Modest, refined, and generous, he had the bearing of a true Confucian. He was promoted to Vice Director of the Court of Justice with the additional title Champion General, then to Regular Attendant of the Palace Library. During Jianyi, after his elder brother Yang died, he raised Yang's orphaned nephews and returned to his home district. At the beginning of Yongxi he was appointed Palace Attendant, Grand General, [11] Left Master of Bright Happiness, and concurrently Director of the Ministry of Justice; soon afterward he also held the post of Supervising Secretary of the Palace Library. In the spring of the third year he lectured on rites in Xianyang Hall by imperial command. Yu held the classics and explained without end; objections flew thick and fast, yet he never lost his easy composure. The Deposed Emperor and all the princes and dukes present sighed in admiration. Soon afterward he died of illness. Posthumously he was ennobled Palace Attendant, Commander of military affairs in Ding, Ji, Xiang, Cang, and Yin provinces, Grand General of Fast Cavalry, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Equal in Honor to the Three Dukes, and Governor of Ding Province.

李沖，字思順，隴西人，敦煌公寶少子也。 少孤，為長兄滎陽太守承所攜訓。 承常言：「此兒器量非恒，方為門戶所寄。 」沖沈雅有大量，隨兄至官。 是時牧守子弟多侵亂民庶，輕有乞奪，沖與承長子韶獨清簡皎然，無所求取，時人美焉。
Li Chong, whose courtesy name was Sishun, came from Longxi and was the youngest son of Duke of Dunhuang Bao. Orphaned in youth, he was raised and instructed by his eldest brother Cheng, Governor of Xingyang. Cheng often said, "This boy's capacity is extraordinary. The fate of our house will rest on him." Chong was deep, refined, and magnanimous. He accompanied his elder brother to his post. At that time the sons of governors and prefects often preyed upon the people, taking what they pleased. Chong and Cheng's eldest son Shao alone remained pure and self-restrained, seeking nothing for themselves, and people praised them for it.

At the end of the Xianzu era he was a student of the Palace Library. Chong cultivated friendships wisely and did not idle in frivolous company; his contemporaries respected him. At the beginning of Emperor Gaozu's reign he was transferred by precedent to Palace Library Cadet, in charge of confidential palace documents. Orderly, diligent, and quick-witted, he gradually won favor and trust. He was promoted to Palace Library Director and Supervising Censor of the Southern Section.

舊無三長，惟立宗主督護，所以民多隱冒，五十、三十家方為一戶。 沖以三正治民，所由來遠，於是創三長之制而上之。 文明太后覽而稱善，引見公卿議之。 中書令鄭羲、祕書令高祐等曰：「沖求立三長者，乃欲混天下一法。 言似可用，事實難行。 」羲又曰：「不信臣言，但試行之，事敗之後，當知愚言之不謬。 」太尉元丕曰：「臣謂此法若行，於公私有益。 」咸稱方今有事之月，校比民戶，新舊未分，民必勞怨，請過今秋，至冬閑月，徐乃遣使，於事為宜，沖曰：「民者，冥也，可使由之，不可使知之。 若不因調時，百姓徒知立長校戶之勤，未見均徭省賦之益，心必生怨。 宜及課調之月，令知賦稅之均。 既識其事，又得其利，因民之欲，為之易行。 」著作郎傅思益進曰：「民俗既異，險易不同，九品差調，為日已久，一旦改法，恐成擾亂。 」太后曰：「立三長，則課有常準，賦有恒分，苞蔭之戶可出，僥倖之人可止，何為而不可？ 」羣議雖有乖異，然惟以變法為難，更無異義。 遂立三長，公私便之。
Formerly there were no three-chiefs; only clan heads and overseers were appointed, so people often hid their numbers and fifty or thirty households were counted as one. Chong held that the three-chiefs system for governing the people was ancient in origin, and so devised the three-chiefs system and submitted it to the throne. Empress Dowager Wenming read it, praised it, and summoned the ministers and dukes to discuss it. Director of the Secretariat Zheng Xi, Palace Library Director Gao You, and others said, "Chong's proposal to establish three chiefs aims to unify the realm under one law. In words it sounds workable; in practice it will be hard to execute." Xi also said, "If Your Majesty does not believe me, try it. When it fails, you will see that my warning was not idle." Grand Commandant Yuan Pi said, "I believe that if this law is enacted, it will benefit both public and private interests." All agreed that in the present busy season, with household registers still being checked and old and new not yet sorted, the people would surely resent the burden. They asked to wait until autumn had passed and dispatch envoys in the winter slack season. Chong said, "The people are simple: they may be led to act, but they must not be made to understand beforehand. If we do not act during the tax season, the people will know only the labor of appointing chiefs and checking households, and not yet see the benefit of equal corvée and lighter levies. Resentment will surely follow. We should act during the tax-assessment month and let them see that the burdens are equal. Once they understand the matter and feel the benefit, the reform will follow their own desire and be easy to enact." Author Gentleman Fu Siyi stepped forward and said, "Customs already differ and terrain varies. The nine-rank system of differential taxation has long stood. To change the law at once may cause turmoil." The empress dowager said, "If three chiefs are established, tax assessment will have a fixed standard and levies a constant share. Hidden households can be exposed and opportunists checked. Why should it not be done?" Though the assembly differed, their objection was only that reform would be difficult; there was no other fundamental dissent. The three-chiefs system was then established, to the benefit of public and private alike.

遷中書令，加散騎常侍，給事中如故。 尋轉南部尚書，賜爵順陽侯。 沖為文明太后所幸，恩寵日盛，賞賜月至數千萬，進爵隴西公，密致珍寶御物以充其第，外人莫得而知焉。 沖家素清貧，於是始為富室。 而謙以自牧，積而能散，近自姻族，逮于鄉閭，莫不分及。 虛己接物，垂念羇寒，衰舊淪屈由之躋敍者，亦以多矣。 時以此稱之。
He was promoted to Director of the Secretariat with the additional title Palace Attendant, retaining his post as Supervising Censor. Soon afterward he was transferred to Director of the Southern Section and ennobled Marquis of Shunyang. Chong won the favor of Empress Dowager Wenming. Honors and gifts mounted month by month until they reached tens of millions. He was advanced to Duke of Longxi, and rare treasures and imperial goods were secretly sent to fill his house—unknown to outsiders. The Li family had always been poor; now for the first time they became rich. Yet he remained humble and self-restrained, gathering wealth only to give it away. From close kin to neighbors, none was left without a share. He humbled himself in all his dealings, looked after the displaced and the poor, and many who had fallen into obscurity and neglect were raised through his patronage. At the time he was widely praised for this.

初，沖兄佐與河南太守來崇同自涼州入國，素有微嫌。 佐因緣成崇罪，餓死獄中。 後崇子護又糾佐贓罪，佐及沖等悉坐幽繫，會赦乃免，佐甚銜之。 至沖寵貴，綜攝內外，護為南部郎，深慮為沖所陷，常求退避，而沖每慰撫之。 護後坐贓罪，懼必不濟。 沖乃具奏與護本末嫌隙，乞原恕之，遂得不坐。 沖從甥陰始孫孤貧，往來沖家，至如子姪。 有人求官，因其納馬於沖，始孫受輒而不為言。 後假方便，借沖此馬，馬主見沖乘馬而不得官，後乃自陳始末。 沖聞之，大驚，執始孫以狀款奏，始孫坐死。 其處要自厲，不念愛惡，皆此類也。
Earlier, Chong's elder brother Zuo and Lai Chong, Administrator of Henan, had entered the realm together from Liangzhou; they had long nursed a slight grudge between them. Zuo seized an opportunity to frame Lai Chong on false charges, and Lai Chong starved to death in prison. Later Lai Chong's son Hu denounced Zuo for corruption. Zuo, Chong, and the others were all imprisoned and were released only when an amnesty was proclaimed. Zuo deeply resented it. When Chong rose to favor and high office and held comprehensive authority at court and beyond, Hu served as a secretary in the Southern Bureau. He greatly feared being ensnared by Chong and constantly sought to withdraw, but Chong always reassured and comforted him. Hu was later implicated in a corruption case and feared he would not escape punishment. Chong then submitted a full memorial recounting his entire history of grievance with Hu and begged that he be pardoned. Hu thus escaped punishment. Chong's maternal nephew Yin Shisun was orphaned and poor. He came and went at Chong's household as freely as sons and nephews. Someone seeking an appointment presented a horse to Chong through him. Shisun accepted it but said nothing. Later, taking advantage of an opportunity, he borrowed the horse from Chong. The owner saw Chong riding it yet failed to obtain an appointment, and afterward reported the whole affair himself. When Chong heard of it he was greatly alarmed. He seized Shisun and submitted a truthful report, and Shisun was sentenced to death. In handling important affairs he held himself to strict standards, setting aside personal likes and dislikes. All his conduct was of this kind.
